title: Thérèse, again
tomorrow: how do you trust something you can't prove?

cards: Habit coaches swear by tiny wins. Floss one tooth. Read one page.
One push-up. Small enough that you can't say no. But they always promise the small thing will grow into a big one.
Thérèse of Lisieux did something odd with the same move. Her small things didn't need to grow. A smile for a sister who grated on her.
Dirty water splashed in her face, taken without a word. She treated them as finished, whole, already enough. So here's the puzzle: how can a chore count for something big if it never gets any bigger?

teach.h: FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.
teach.b: Jesus leaves a clue in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater." Look at what he doesn't say.
He doesn't say the least turns into the greater.
He says it's the same faithfulness. The size changes; the person doesn't. Thérèse pushes that one step further.
In her Story of a Soul she says, in effect, that Jesus looks less at how great or how hard an action is than at the love it's done with. That's the puzzle solved. The measure was never the chore.
It's the love inside the chore, and love doesn't come in sizes. A folded towel and a lifetime of service can hold the same thing. Her name for it was the little way.
And it's honest about a catch: little doesn't mean easy.
A small thing done with great love, again, on a tired afternoon, for someone who won't notice, may be the hardest kind of small there is.
One detail to tell a friend tonight: Thérèse pictured herself as a little flower, and was glad to stay one. Small wasn't a stage she was trying to get past.
Back on the climb, we walked through her whole story, the splashes and the petals. Today, from near the summit, just its shape.

how: Catholics remember Thérèse of Lisieux on October 1, and many follow her little way by offering ordinary tasks and small kindnesses to God, done with love.

s: the little way means holiness is easy
little isn't easy: a small thing done with great love, again and again, is hard.
in Luke, Jesus ties faithfulness in the least to faithfulness in the greater
"faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater."
for Thérèse, small acts were practice for big ones later
she treated small things as whole; the love in them was the measure, not their size.

games.q: your little brother wants help with his puzzle, the third time today. you're tired, and it's tiny. on the little way, what makes it count?
o: only whether it helps him finish faster.
the love you bring to it, even tired.
nothing yet; save your love for bigger asks.
games.why: for Thérèse, Jesus looks less at the size of an act than at the love it's done with. the tired, tiny yes counts.

practice: Pick one small thing within reach: a cup to rinse, a blanket to fold, a shoe to set straight. Do it slowly, as if for someone you love, then sit back down with it done.
If you pray, you can offer it the way Thérèse did, a small thing given whole.

wordCard.voice: Thérèse. Thérèse of Lisieux, the young Carmelite whose little way measures a day by love, not by size.

orig.note: French, written in Latin letters: the little way, the name readers give Thérèse's path.

carryVoice: The line to keep: little things, great love, since the size of the thing was never the point. See you tomorrow.
